lessons.title: Tables, rows and columns
lessons.explanation: A table is a structured set of rows and columns. Before writing SQL, identify the row grain: what one row represents.
lessons.scenario: A commerce analyst receives an orders table where each row is one order.
lessons.workedExample: orders(order_id, customer_id, status, revenue) — one row = one order.
lessons.question: Which statement correctly describes the grain?
options: One row represents one customer forever.
hints: Focus on the core idea: tables, rows and columns.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
The order_id identifies each row, so the grain is one order.
lessons.solution: The order_id identifies each row, so the grain is one order.

lessons.title: SELECT only what you need
lessons.explanation: SELECT chooses columns. Listing only required columns makes queries easier to read and reduces unnecessary data exposure.
lessons.scenario: A merchandising manager asks for order_id and revenue, not every field.
lessons.workedExample: SELECT order_id, revenue FROM orders;
lessons.question: Which query returns only order_id and revenue?
hints: Focus on the core idea: select only what you need.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Use SELECT order_id, revenue FROM orders;
lessons.solution: Use SELECT order_id, revenue FROM orders;

lessons.title: Filter rows with WHERE
lessons.explanation: WHERE keeps rows that match a condition. Filters should reflect the business definition exactly.
lessons.scenario: A bank operations team wants transactions already routed for review.
lessons.workedExample: SELECT transaction_id FROM bank_transactions WHERE review_flag = 1;
lessons.question: Which clause limits the result to review_flag = 1?
hints: Focus on the core idea: filter rows with where.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Use WHERE review_flag = 1.
lessons.solution: Use WHERE review_flag = 1.

lessons.title: Sort and limit results
lessons.explanation: ORDER BY controls sort order. DESC means largest first; LIMIT keeps the requested number of rows.
lessons.scenario: A logistics manager wants the five most expensive shipments.
lessons.workedExample: SELECT shipment_id, shipping_cost FROM logistics_shipments ORDER BY shipping_cost DESC LIMIT 5;
lessons.question: What combination returns the five highest costs?
hints: Focus on the core idea: sort and limit results.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Use ORDER BY shipping_cost DESC LIMIT 5.
lessons.solution: Use ORDER BY shipping_cost DESC LIMIT 5.

lessons.title: COUNT, SUM and AVG
lessons.explanation: Aggregate functions summarize many rows: COUNT counts, SUM totals, AVG calculates a mean.
lessons.scenario: Hospital operations needs total arrivals and average wait time for a reporting period.
lessons.workedExample: SELECT SUM(arrivals), AVG(avg_wait_minutes) FROM hospital_daily_ops;
lessons.question: Which function calculates average wait time?
hints: Focus on the core idea: count, sum and avg.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Use AVG(avg_wait_minutes).
lessons.solution: Use AVG(avg_wait_minutes).

lessons.title: GROUP BY business segments
lessons.explanation: GROUP BY changes the grain from individual rows to one row per group and lets aggregate functions summarize each group.
lessons.scenario: A SaaS finance team wants MRR by customer segment.
lessons.workedExample: SELECT segment, SUM(mrr) AS total_mrr FROM accounts GROUP BY segment;
lessons.question: Why is GROUP BY segment required here?
options: To return one aggregated result per segment.
lessons.correctAnswer: To return one aggregated result per segment.
hints: Focus on the core idea: group by business segments.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
GROUP BY segment creates one aggregate row per segment.
lessons.solution: GROUP BY segment creates one aggregate row per segment.

lessons.title: JOIN related tables
lessons.explanation: JOIN combines related tables using a key. Use the relationship key, not a convenient-looking text field.
lessons.scenario: An analyst needs order revenue plus each customer's region from separate orders and customers tables.
lessons.workedExample: SELECT o.order_id, c.region, o.revenue FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;
lessons.question: Which join condition is defensible?
hints: Focus on the core idea: join related tables.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Join on the shared customer_id key.
lessons.solution: Join on the shared customer_id key.

lessons.title: CASE, CTEs and window thinking
lessons.explanation: CASE creates business categories, CTEs organize multi-step logic, and window functions calculate across related rows without collapsing detail.
lessons.scenario: A senior analyst must bucket accounts by MRR and later rank them within segment.
lessons.workedExample: WITH base AS (...) SELECT ..., ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY segment ORDER BY mrr DESC) AS rank_in_segment FROM base;
lessons.question: Which feature ranks rows while keeping each account row visible?
options: A window function such as ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...)
GROUP BY without selecting account rows
lessons.correctAnswer: A window function such as ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...)
hints: Focus on the core idea: case, ctes and window thinking.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Use a window function such as ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) to rank without collapsing rows.
lessons.solution: Use a window function such as ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) to rank without collapsing rows.

lessons.title: Cells, rows and references
lessons.explanation: Spreadsheet formulas refer to cells by address. Columns use letters and rows use numbers.
lessons.scenario: A sales workbook stores unit price in B2 and quantity in C2.
lessons.workedExample: B2 means column B, row 2.
lessons.question: What does C2 identify?
hints: Focus on the core idea: cells, rows and references.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
C2 is column C, row 2.
lessons.solution: C2 is column C, row 2.

lessons.title: Arithmetic formulas
lessons.explanation: Formulas begin with = and combine cell references with operators such as +, -, * and /.
lessons.scenario: A sales analyst needs line revenue from price × quantity.
lessons.question: Which formula calculates price in B2 times quantity in C2?
hints: Focus on the core idea: arithmetic formulas.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Use =B2*C2.
lessons.solution: Use =B2*C2.

lessons.title: Relative and absolute references
lessons.explanation: Relative references move when copied. Absolute references such as $F$1 stay fixed.
lessons.scenario: A pricing model copies a formula down many rows while the tax rate stays in cell F1.
lessons.question: Which reference keeps the tax-rate cell fixed?
hints: Focus on the core idea: relative and absolute references.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Use $F$1 to lock both column and row.
lessons.solution: Use $F$1 to lock both column and row.

lessons.title: IF for business rules
lessons.explanation: IF evaluates a condition and returns one value when true and another when false.
lessons.scenario: A review sheet should label balances above 100000 as High.
lessons.workedExample: =IF(B2>100000,"High","Normal")
lessons.question: Which function expresses this two-outcome business rule?
hints: Focus on the core idea: if for business rules.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Use IF(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false).
lessons.solution: Use IF(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false).

lessons.title: Lookups across tables
lessons.explanation: XLOOKUP (or INDEX/MATCH in older workflows) retrieves a related value using a key.
lessons.scenario: A shipment sheet has warehouse_id and a second table maps each warehouse to its city.
lessons.workedExample: =XLOOKUP(A2,Warehouses!A:A,Warehouses!B:B,"Unknown")
lessons.question: What should be used as the lookup key?
hints: Focus on the core idea: lookups across tables.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Use the stable warehouse_id as the lookup key.
lessons.solution: Use the stable warehouse_id as the lookup key.

lessons.title: SUMIFS and COUNTIFS
lessons.explanation: SUMIFS sums values meeting one or more conditions; COUNTIFS counts rows meeting conditions.
lessons.scenario: Operations wants total arrivals for Saturdays only.
lessons.workedExample: =SUMIFS(B:B,A:A,"Saturday")
lessons.question: Which function sums arrivals only when day is Saturday?
hints: Focus on the core idea: sumifs and countifs.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Use SUMIFS because the task is a conditional sum.
lessons.solution: Use SUMIFS because the task is a conditional sum.

lessons.title: Sort and filter safely
lessons.explanation: Filters hide rows that do not meet conditions; sorting changes display order. Neither should silently alter the underlying values.
lessons.scenario: A manager asks to inspect completed orders above ₹5,000.
lessons.workedExample: Filter status=completed and revenue>5000, then sort revenue descending.
lessons.question: What is the safest first action?
options: Apply explicit filters that match the requested business definition.
lessons.correctAnswer: Apply explicit filters that match the requested business definition.
hints: Focus on the core idea: sort and filter safely.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Apply reversible filters that match the business definition, then sort if useful.
lessons.solution: Apply reversible filters that match the business definition, then sort if useful.

lessons.title: Pivot tables
lessons.explanation: A pivot table summarizes data by dimensions and measures. First confirm row grain, then choose rows/columns and the aggregation.
lessons.scenario: Finance wants MRR by segment and plan without writing many formulas.
lessons.workedExample: Rows=segment, Columns=plan, Values=SUM of MRR.
lessons.question: What belongs in Values for total MRR?
hints: Focus on the core idea: pivot tables.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Use SUM of MRR in the Values area.
lessons.solution: Use SUM of MRR in the Values area.

lessons.title: Start with data grain
lessons.explanation: Before deleting duplicates, define what one row should represent. Duplicate-looking rows may be valid at a different grain.
lessons.scenario: A vendor file contains repeated order IDs, but some orders legitimately have multiple line items.
lessons.workedExample: If one row is an order line, order_id alone is not a unique key; order_id + line_id may be.
lessons.question: What should you confirm before deduplication?
options: The intended row grain and business key.
Which row has the largest revenue.
lessons.correctAnswer: The intended row grain and business key.
hints: Focus on the core idea: start with data grain.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Confirm the intended row grain and business key before deleting anything.
lessons.solution: Confirm the intended row grain and business key before deleting anything.

lessons.title: Handle missing values by meaning
lessons.explanation: Missing values are not all the same. Fill with 0 only when the business meaning truly means none; otherwise preserve Unknown or investigate.
lessons.scenario: Some support_ticket_count values are blank because no tickets were logged; plan_name blanks mean unknown plan.
lessons.workedExample: support_ticket_count null → 0 when source semantics confirm no ticket; plan_name null → Unknown.
lessons.question: Should every missing numeric field automatically become 0?
options: No. Imputation must follow the field's business meaning.
lessons.correctAnswer: No. Imputation must follow the field's business meaning.
hints: Focus on the core idea: handle missing values by meaning.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Do not default every blank to zero; use the documented business meaning.
lessons.solution: Do not default every blank to zero; use the documented business meaning.

lessons.title: Remove true duplicates
lessons.explanation: Deduplicate only when a uniqueness rule is known. Keep an audit count of removed rows.
lessons.scenario: A transaction export accidentally contains the exact same transaction_id twice.
lessons.workedExample: If transaction_id is guaranteed unique, repeated transaction_id rows should be investigated and one canonical record retained.
lessons.question: What makes a duplicate safe to remove?
options: A validated uniqueness rule plus matching duplicate evidence.
They occur next to each other.
lessons.correctAnswer: A validated uniqueness rule plus matching duplicate evidence.
hints: Focus on the core idea: remove true duplicates.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Use a validated uniqueness rule and keep an audit trail.
lessons.solution: Use a validated uniqueness rule and keep an audit trail.

lessons.title: Fix types and dates
lessons.explanation: Standardize dates to one parseable format and validate ambiguous values before conversion.
lessons.scenario: A date column mixes 2026-10-07 and 07/10/2026.
lessons.question: Why is 01/02/2026 risky without locale context?
options: It can mean different dates under different day/month conventions.
It cannot be stored as text.
lessons.correctAnswer: It can mean different dates under different day/month conventions.
hints: Focus on the core idea: fix types and dates.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Validate the source date convention before normalizing to a single format.
lessons.solution: Validate the source date convention before normalizing to a single format.

lessons.title: Normalize categories
lessons.explanation: Normalize whitespace and case, then map only known aliases to canonical labels.
lessons.scenario: The same route status appears as Late, late, LATE and ' late '.
lessons.workedExample: trim → lowercase → map to canonical status.
lessons.question: What is the purpose of category normalization?
options: To make equivalent labels group together consistently.
lessons.correctAnswer: To make equivalent labels group together consistently.
hints: Focus on the core idea: normalize categories.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Normalize known variants so equivalent labels group together.
lessons.solution: Normalize known variants so equivalent labels group together.

lessons.title: Validate impossible values
lessons.explanation: Domain rules catch values that are syntactically valid but business-impossible.
lessons.scenario: A refund_amount field contains -500 even though refunds are stored as positive amounts.
lessons.workedExample: If refunds must be non-negative, -500 should be quarantined or corrected from source evidence.
lessons.question: What should happen to an impossible value?
options: Flag it for validation rather than silently guessing a replacement.
Replace it with the average automatically.
Ignore it because it is numeric.
lessons.correctAnswer: Flag it for validation rather than silently guessing a replacement.
hints: Focus on the core idea: validate impossible values.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Flag business-impossible values and validate them against source evidence.
lessons.solution: Flag business-impossible values and validate them against source evidence.

lessons.title: Treat outliers carefully
lessons.explanation: An outlier is unusual, not automatically wrong. Investigate whether it is valid before excluding it.
lessons.scenario: Most contracts are ₹20k–₹80k MRR, but one enterprise account is ₹900k.
lessons.workedExample: Use boxplots/IQR or robust percentiles to detect unusual values, then verify business context.
lessons.question: Should the ₹900k account be deleted immediately?
options: No. Verify whether it is a valid enterprise account before deciding how to analyze it.
Yes, every outlier is an error.
lessons.correctAnswer: No. Verify whether it is a valid enterprise account before deciding how to analyze it.
hints: Focus on the core idea: treat outliers carefully.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Validate the outlier first; use robust summaries if it is legitimate.
lessons.solution: Validate the outlier first; use robust summaries if it is legitimate.

lessons.title: Document quality controls
lessons.explanation: A reproducible cleaning process records rules, row counts, exceptions and assumptions so another analyst can repeat it.
lessons.scenario: Two analysts clean the same monthly file differently and produce conflicting totals.
lessons.workedExample: Log: source rows, duplicate rows removed, missing treatment, invalid values, final rows.
lessons.question: What makes cleaning auditable?
options: Documented rules and before/after quality counts.
lessons.correctAnswer: Documented rules and before/after quality counts.
hints: Focus on the core idea: document quality controls.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Keep documented rules and before/after quality counts.
lessons.solution: Keep documented rules and before/after quality counts.

lessons.title: Population, sample and variable types
lessons.explanation: The population is the full group you care about; a sample is the subset observed. Variable type affects which summaries and tests make sense.
lessons.scenario: An e-commerce company has 2 million customers but surveys 2,000 about delivery satisfaction.
lessons.workedExample: Population = all 2M customers; sample = surveyed 2,000.
lessons.question: What is the sample?
options: Only customers who gave the highest score.
hints: Focus on the core idea: population, sample and variable types.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
The 2,000 surveyed customers are the sample.
lessons.solution: The 2,000 surveyed customers are the sample.

lessons.title: Mean, median and mode
lessons.explanation: Mean uses every magnitude, median is the middle ordered value, and mode is the most frequent value. Extreme values can pull the mean.
lessons.workedExample: Median = ₹700; the mean is much larger because of ₹7,500.
lessons.question: Which measure best represents the typical order here?
hints: Focus on the core idea: mean, median and mode.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Use the median because it is robust to the extreme ₹7,500 order.
lessons.solution: Use the median because it is robust to the extreme ₹7,500 order.

lessons.title: Range, variance and standard deviation
lessons.explanation: Spread measures variability. Range uses max-min; variance averages squared deviations; standard deviation returns to the original unit.
lessons.scenario: Two hospital days have the same average wait but one has very inconsistent waits.
lessons.workedExample: Average 40 min with SD 4 is more consistent than average 40 min with SD 20.
lessons.question: Which statistic directly communicates typical spread in minutes?
hints: Focus on the core idea: range, variance and standard deviation.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Standard deviation communicates spread in the original unit, minutes.
lessons.solution: Standard deviation communicates spread in the original unit, minutes.

lessons.title: Quartiles, percentiles and outliers
lessons.explanation: Percentiles describe the value below which a percentage of observations fall. P90 exposes long-tail service experience that the median can hide.
lessons.scenario: Median transit time is 24 hours but P90 is 62 hours.
lessons.workedExample: P90=62 means about 90% of shipments are at or below 62 hours.
lessons.question: What does P90 help reveal?
options: Long-tail performance experienced by the slowest portion of shipments.
The exact cause of every delay.
lessons.correctAnswer: Long-tail performance experienced by the slowest portion of shipments.
hints: Focus on the core idea: quartiles, percentiles and outliers.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Use high percentiles to monitor tail service performance.
lessons.solution: Use high percentiles to monitor tail service performance.

lessons.title: Distributions and skew
lessons.explanation: A distribution shows how values are spread. A long high-value tail creates right skew; median and percentiles may be more useful than mean alone.
lessons.scenario: Most support tickets resolve within 1–2 days but a few take 15 days.
lessons.workedExample: Resolution time is likely right-skewed.
lessons.question: Which shape is most plausible?
hints: Focus on the core idea: distributions and skew.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Rare much-larger values create a right-skewed distribution.
lessons.solution: Rare much-larger values create a right-skewed distribution.

lessons.title: Probability, sampling and the CLT
lessons.explanation: Probability quantifies uncertainty. Random sampling reduces selection bias. Larger samples often stabilize estimates, but large biased samples are still biased.
lessons.scenario: A bank samples transactions to estimate the review-flag rate rather than checking every historical transaction.
lessons.workedExample: A larger representative sample usually gives a more stable estimate than a tiny convenience sample.
lessons.question: What matters more than simply having a large sample?
options: The sample should also represent the population and avoid systematic bias.
Only the first records should be sampled.
lessons.correctAnswer: The sample should also represent the population and avoid systematic bias.
hints: Focus on the core idea: probability, sampling and the clt.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Use representative sampling; sample size alone cannot fix systematic bias.
lessons.solution: Use representative sampling; sample size alone cannot fix systematic bias.

lessons.title: Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests
lessons.explanation: A confidence interval gives a plausible range for an effect. A hypothesis test evaluates compatibility with a null model. A p-value is not the probability the null is true.
lessons.scenario: Average wait fell by 5 minutes after a scheduling change, but daily variation is high.
lessons.workedExample: Report effect size and interval; check assumptions before declaring a change.
lessons.question: If p=0.18, what is the safest conclusion at a 0.05 threshold?
options: The evidence is insufficient to reject the null; the observed difference may still be practically interesting and needs more evidence.
The new schedule is definitely better.
lessons.correctAnswer: The evidence is insufficient to reject the null; the observed difference may still be practically interesting and needs more evidence.
hints: Focus on the core idea: confidence intervals and hypothesis tests.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Call the result inconclusive rather than treating p>0.05 as proof of no effect.
lessons.solution: Call the result inconclusive rather than treating p>0.05 as proof of no effect.

lessons.title: Correlation, regression and A/B tests
lessons.explanation: Correlation measures association, not causation. Regression can adjust for measured factors; randomized A/B tests are stronger for causal questions. Power controls what effect sizes can be detected reliably.
lessons.scenario: Customers attending training retain more often, but larger customers also attend more training.
lessons.workedExample: Segment/control for account size or run a randomized experiment before claiming training caused retention.
lessons.question: What is the strongest statement from the observed correlation alone?
options: Training attendance is associated with retention, but other factors may explain part of the relationship.
lessons.correctAnswer: Training attendance is associated with retention, but other factors may explain part of the relationship.
hints: Focus on the core idea: correlation, regression and a/b tests.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
State association, identify confounders, and use stronger experimental design for causal claims.
lessons.solution: State association, identify confounders, and use stronger experimental design for causal claims.

lessons.title: DataFrames and Series
lessons.explanation: A DataFrame is a two-dimensional table; a Series is usually one column. Inspect shape, columns, data types and sample rows before transforming data.
lessons.scenario: An analyst loads an orders CSV into Pandas.
lessons.workedExample: df.shape, df.dtypes, df.head()
lessons.question: What does df.head() help you do?
options: Preview the first rows and understand the dataset structure.
lessons.correctAnswer: Preview the first rows and understand the dataset structure.
hints: Focus on the core idea: dataframes and series.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Use df.head() to inspect sample rows.
lessons.solution: Use df.head() to inspect sample rows.

lessons.title: Select columns and filter rows
lessons.explanation: Boolean filtering keeps rows that satisfy a condition; double brackets select multiple columns.
lessons.scenario: Growth needs only completed orders and the order_id/revenue columns.
lessons.workedExample: df[df['status']=='completed'][['order_id','revenue']]
lessons.question: Which part filters completed rows?
hints: Focus on the core idea: select columns and filter rows.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Use the boolean condition df['status']=='completed' inside df[...].
lessons.solution: Use the boolean condition df['status']=='completed' inside df[...].

lessons.title: Missing values
lessons.explanation: Use isna() to inspect missingness. fillna() is appropriate only when the replacement has a defensible business meaning; dropna() can bias results.
lessons.scenario: A CRM export contains missing plan names and missing support counts.
lessons.workedExample: df['plan']=df['plan'].fillna('Unknown') when Unknown is the documented meaning.
lessons.question: Which command explicitly fills missing plan names?
hints: Focus on the core idea: missing values.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Use fillna with the intended replacement value.
lessons.solution: Use fillna with the intended replacement value.

lessons.title: Create derived columns
lessons.explanation: Vectorized column arithmetic creates a new metric for all rows without a Python loop.
lessons.scenario: Marketing needs conversion rate from conversions and clicks.
lessons.workedExample: df['conversion_rate']=df['conversions']/df['clicks']*100
lessons.question: What is the denominator of conversion rate here?
hints: Focus on the core idea: create derived columns.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Rate = outcomes divided by opportunities, so clicks are the denominator.
lessons.solution: Rate = outcomes divided by opportunities, so clicks are the denominator.

lessons.title: GroupBy and aggregation
lessons.explanation: groupby() splits rows into groups and sum(), mean() or count() summarizes each group.
lessons.scenario: Finance wants total MRR by segment.
lessons.workedExample: df.groupby('segment')['mrr'].sum()
lessons.question: Which method creates one total per segment?
hints: Focus on the core idea: groupby and aggregation.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Group by segment, then sum MRR.
lessons.solution: Group by segment, then sum MRR.

lessons.title: Sort and top-N
lessons.explanation: sort_values() orders rows; head(n) selects the first n after sorting.
lessons.scenario: Operations wants the ten most expensive shipments.
lessons.workedExample: df.sort_values('shipping_cost',ascending=False).head(10)
lessons.question: Why must ascending=False be used?
options: To place the highest shipping costs first.
lessons.correctAnswer: To place the highest shipping costs first.
hints: Focus on the core idea: sort and top-n.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Sort descending, then take head(10).
lessons.solution: Sort descending, then take head(10).

lessons.title: Merge DataFrames
lessons.explanation: merge() joins DataFrames using one or more keys. Validate join cardinality so a supposed many-to-one join does not multiply rows unexpectedly.
lessons.scenario: Transactions contain account_id while a separate accounts table contains segment.
lessons.workedExample: transactions.merge(accounts,on='account_id',how='left',validate='many_to_one')
lessons.question: What should be checked after a merge?
hints: Focus on the core idea: merge dataframes.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Validate join cardinality, row counts and unmatched keys.
lessons.solution: Validate join cardinality, row counts and unmatched keys.

lessons.title: Dates, pivots and method chaining
lessons.explanation: Convert date text with to_datetime(), derive time fields, aggregate or pivot, and chain transformations when it stays readable.
lessons.scenario: Operations needs monthly arrivals by department from daily records.
lessons.workedExample: df.assign(date=pd.to_datetime(df['date'])).pivot_table(index='month',columns='department',values='arrivals',aggfunc='sum')
lessons.question: What should happen before extracting month from a date string?
options: Parse it to a datetime with validated format/semantics.
lessons.correctAnswer: Parse it to a datetime with validated format/semantics.
hints: Focus on the core idea: dates, pivots and method chaining.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Parse and validate the date column before datetime operations.
lessons.solution: Parse and validate the date column before datetime operations.

lessons.title: Start with the decision
lessons.explanation: A dashboard should answer a decision question, not display every available metric. Clarify audience, decision, time horizon and data grain first.
lessons.scenario: A CEO asks for a dashboard about revenue growth.
lessons.workedExample: Decision: Is revenue growth coming from more orders or higher order value?
lessons.question: What should you define before choosing charts?
options: The business decision the dashboard must support.
lessons.correctAnswer: The business decision the dashboard must support.
hints: Focus on the core idea: start with the decision.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Define the audience and business decision before choosing charts.
lessons.solution: Define the audience and business decision before choosing charts.

lessons.title: Define KPIs precisely
lessons.explanation: A KPI needs a formula, grain, time window, inclusion/exclusion rules and owner. Without a shared definition, dashboards can disagree while both calculations are internally correct.
lessons.scenario: Product and Finance disagree on what 'active customer' means.
lessons.workedExample: Monthly active account = account with qualifying product activity during calendar month, excluding test accounts.
lessons.question: What prevents KPI-definition conflicts?
options: A documented metric definition including grain, window and filters.
lessons.correctAnswer: A documented metric definition including grain, window and filters.
hints: Focus on the core idea: define kpis precisely.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Document the KPI formula, grain, time window and filters.
lessons.solution: Document the KPI formula, grain, time window and filters.

lessons.title: Line charts vs bar charts
lessons.explanation: Line charts are strong for ordered time trends. Bar charts are strong for comparing discrete categories.
lessons.scenario: Network leaders need monthly on-time delivery trend and route comparisons.
lessons.workedExample: Use line for monthly SLA trend; bars for route-level SLA comparison.
lessons.question: Which chart best shows a 12-month trend?
hints: Focus on the core idea: line charts vs bar charts.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Use a line chart for an ordered time trend.
lessons.solution: Use a line chart for an ordered time trend.

lessons.title: Scatter plots and distributions
lessons.explanation: Scatter plots show relationships between two numeric variables. Histograms/boxplots show distributions and outliers.
lessons.scenario: Marketing asks whether spend and conversions move together, while operations asks about the shape of resolution times.
lessons.workedExample: Scatter: spend vs conversions; histogram/boxplot: resolution time.
lessons.question: Which chart helps inspect a relationship between spend and conversions?
hints: Focus on the core idea: scatter plots and distributions.
Use the company scenario and worked example before guessing.
Use a scatter plot for two paired numeric variables.
lessons.solution: Use a scatter plot for two paired numeric variables.

lessons.title: Avoid misleading visuals
lessons.explanation: Visual scales, denominators and labels can exaggerate differences. Bar charts generally need a meaningful zero baseline.
lessons.scenario: A bar chart of wait time starts the y-axis at 48 minutes, making a 2-minute change look enormous.
lessons.workedExample: Show axis range clearly and avoid visually overstating a small operational change.

lessons.title: Retention, churn and NRR
lessons.explanation: NRR includes churn, contraction and expansion: (start - churn - contraction + expansion)/start.

Revenue is guaranteed to grow forever.

lessons.explanation: CAC = acquisition spend / customers acquired. LTV estimates customer value; payback asks how long gross profit takes to recover CAC.

lessons.title: Forecasts and scenarios
lessons.explanation: Forecasts are estimates with error, not promises. Validate against history, model seasonality, and present scenarios/ranges when uncertainty matters.

lessons.workedExample: Base 100k shipments; downside 92k; upside 112k with stated assumptions.

lessons.title: Write a decision-ready insight
lessons.explanation: Strong analyst writing uses finding → evidence → bounded interpretation → recommendation → business impact. Do not claim causes the data cannot establish.

lessons.workedExample: Median wait improved from 46 to 39 minutes, but P90 remains 88; typical experience improved while the long tail persists.

lessons.title: Stakeholders, ethics and prioritization
lessons.explanation: Good analytics balances usefulness with privacy, fairness, governance and uncertainty. Minimize sensitive data, challenge unsupported proxies and communicate limitations.
lessons.scenario: A leader asks for a customer-risk list using a weak proxy and wants it emailed broadly.
lessons.workedExample: Use approved fields, restrict access, validate the signal, and avoid treating a review flag as proof of wrongdoing.

options: Escalate/validate it and avoid using it as a definitive decision rule.
Use it silently because leadership asked.
lessons.correctAnswer: Escalate/validate it and avoid using it as a definitive decision rule.
